content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a report in 2012 addressing various aspects of male circumcision. 2. Siegfried N. and colleagues conducted a systematic review in 2009, published in the Cochrane Database, evaluating the role of male circumcision in preventing heterosexual acquisition of HIV in men. 3. The Global Harmonization Task Force Study Group 5 released a 2012 report on reportable events during pre-market clinical investigations. 4. Cheng YA proposed a standardized protocol for adult male circumcision using the Chinese Shang Ring, reporting outcomes from 328 cases in China in 2009, published in the National Journal of Andrology. 5. Li H-N compared the clinical effectiveness of Shang Ring circumcision versus conventional surgical methods in a 2010 study published in the National Journal of Andrology. 6. Peng YF and colleagues, in a 2008 study in the Asian Journal of Andrology, explored the clinical application of a new minimally invasive circumcision device. 7. Peng YF et al. reported in 2010 that standardized male circumcision using the Shang Ring reduced postoperative complications, based on 351 cases. 8. Yan B and colleagues evaluated the outcomes of Shang Ring circumcision in children, analyzing 824 cases in a 2010 study published in the National Journal of Andrology. 9. Barone MA et al. conducted a randomized trial in 2012, published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, examining the Shang Ring for adult male circumcision with delayed removal leading to detachment. 10. Barone MA et al. also conducted a proof-of-concept study in Kenya in 2011, evaluating the Shang Ring device for adult male circumcision. 11. Kigozi G et al. assessed the acceptability and safety of the Shang Ring for adult male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, in a study published in 2013. 12. Sokal DC et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2013 comparing the Shang Ring to conventional surgical techniques for adult male circumcision, focusing on safety and acceptability. 13. Sokal DC et al. also performed a field study in Kenya and Zambia, evaluating the Shang Ring in routine clinical settings, as reported to the WHO Technical Advisory Group in 2012. 14. FHI 360 published a 2011 statistical report evaluating healing times and spontaneous detachment potential of the Shang Ring. 15. A randomized controlled trial comparing the Shang Ring to conventional surgical methods for adult male circumcision in Kenya and Zambia was presented at the XIX International AIDS Conference in 2012. 16. FHI 360 conducted a prospective observational study in 2012 on the use of the Shang Ring in routine clinical settings in Kenya and Zambia. 17. Bitega JP et al. evaluated the safety and efficacy of the PrePex device for rapid scale-up of male circumcision in resource-limited settings for HIV prevention, publishing their findings in 2011. 18. Mutabazi V et al. conducted a prospective cohort field study in 2012 to assess the safety and efficacy of the PrePex device for non-surgical circumcision performed by nurses in resource-limited settings. 19. Tshimanga M et al. compared the PrePex device to forceps-guided surgical circumcision in a randomized trial in Zimbabwe, with findings reported in 2013. 20. Tshimanga M et al. also conducted a Phase I safety trial and a Phase III cohort field study in Zimbabwe in 2013, evaluating the PrePex device for male circumcision performed by nurses. 21. Mutabazi V et al. published a 2012 study comparing non-surgical devices to surgical techniques for male circumcision in resource-limited settings, focusing on HIV prevention. 22. Galukande M et al. released an interim report in 2013 on the safety of a non-surgical device for adult male circumcision without injected anesthesia in non-sterile settings. 23. Kigozi G evaluated the acceptability and safety of the PrePex device for male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, in a 2013 study. 24. Hallett T et al. published new estimates in 2011 on the population impact of circumcision interventions on HIV prevention for both men and women. 25. Hewett PC et al. assessed the resumption of sexual activity during the post-circumcision wound-healing period in a 2013 study. 26. Herman-Roloff A et al. identified factors associated with early resumption of sexual activity following medical male circumcision in Kenya, publishing their findings in 2012. 27. The Government of Kenya released a progress report in 2012 on the country’s voluntary medical male circumcision program from 2008 to 2010. 28. Lissouba P et al. developed a model for rolling out comprehensive adult male circumcision services in African low-income settings with high HIV incidence, published in 2010. 29. Bratt JH and Zyambo Z compared the direct costs of Shang Ring circumcision to standard surgical techniques in Zambia in a 2013 study. 30. Duffy K et al. evaluated the reach and cost-effectiveness of the PrePex device for safe male circumcision in Uganda, publishing their findings in 2013. 31. Obiero W et al. analyzed the cost implications of the PrePex device compared to forceps-guided methods in sub-Saharan Africa, concluding it is unlikely to achieve cost savings, as reported in 2013. 32. Njeuhmeli E et al. conducted a cost analysis in 2013 on integrating the PrePex device into Zimbabwe’s voluntary medical male circumcision program. 33. WHO/ExpandNet published a 2011 guideline on planning pilot projects for successful scaling up of male circumcision devices for HIV prevention. 34. Dickson KE et al. analyzed policy and program implementation for voluntary medical male circumcision in Eastern and Southern Africa in a 2011 study. 35. Mwandi Z et al. documented the rapid expansion of male circumcision services in Kenya from 2008 to 2011, translating research into practice. 36. ISO 13485 outlined quality management system requirements for medical devices in a 2003 publication. 37. Odeny TA et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial in 2012 to evaluate the use of text messaging to improve attendance at post-operative clinic visits after adult male circumcision. 38. 39. PEPFAR published a 2012 guide on best practices for voluntary medical male circumcision site operations. 40. Plotkin M et al. examined social and individual factors affecting attendance at male circumcision services in Tanzania in a 2013 study. 41. UNAIDS released a 2010 guidance note on developing communication strategies for male circumcision programs. 42. Rogers E published the fifth edition of Diffusion of Innovations in 2003, providing insights into the adoption of new practices. 43. Herman-Roloff A et al. evaluated the acceptability of medical male circumcision among uncircumcised men in Kenya one year after the launch of the national program, publishing their findings in 2011. 44. Khumalo-Sakutukwa G et al. explored socio-cultural barriers to medical male circumcision in traditionally non-circumcising rural communities in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2013 study. 45. Ssekubugu R et al. identified contextual barriers and motivators for adult male circumcision in Rakai, Uganda, in a 2013 qualitative study. 46. Chrouser K et al. 47. The Global Harmonization Task Force Study Group 2 published global guidance in 2000 on adverse reporting for medical devices in post-market surveillance. 48. WHO released a 2012 report on the use of devices for adult male circumcision in public health HIV prevention programs, summarizing conclusions from the technical advisory group on innovations in male circumcision.
